sensitivity_cases.label: Adopted model (the scenarios)
sensitivity_cases.change_as_recorded: adopted: pooled revision (ii) cap+A2, configuration A, Madison on the Madison-like path; lower = mean of Rhode Island and Oregon; Milwaukee at its measured 2022-2025 rate

sensitivity_cases.label: Lower scenario at the 10th percentile of the state spread (Gate 3 definition)
sensitivity_cases.what: The lower scenario is set at the 10th percentile of how much the eight statewide-law states' levels differ (every place's central level divided by 1.885), as at Gate 3, instead of the average of the two slowest states, Rhode Island and Oregon. That level is below every statewide-law state's. Only the lower changes.
sensitivity_cases.change_as_recorded: Lower as a statistical 10th percentile of the between-state spread (the Gate 3 lower: central levels / 1.885)

sensitivity_cases.label: Madison on the statewide estimate, like every other place
sensitivity_cases.what: Madison follows the statewide estimate for places like it instead of the path that similar cities in Washington and Oregon took. This changes Madison's addition only, and through it the statewide total.
sensitivity_cases.change_as_recorded: Madison at its pooled level (no Madison-like path)

sensitivity_cases.label: Leave California out of the typical level
sensitivity_cases.what: The eight states' typical level is set without California. The central falls, and Strong adoption falls most, because California is the state that stretches the range upward. This alternative predicted the held-out states less well. The lower is the same Rhode Island and Oregon average, taken from this fit.
sensitivity_cases.change_as_recorded: California out of the common level (configuration B)

sensitivity_cases.label: A stricter correction for California's ADUs on apartment properties
sensitivity_cases.what: California's counts include ADUs on apartment and other multifamily properties, which the benchmark law does not allow. This removes more of them, using Los Angeles County parcel records. The lower is the same Rhode Island and Oregon average, taken from this fit.
sensitivity_cases.change_as_recorded: LA-calibrated multifamily correction (option iii, configuration A)

sensitivity_cases.label: No slow start: full effect from 2027
sensitivity_cases.what: In the adopted model the law reaches about 63%, 80% and 82% of its full effect in 2027, 2028 and 2029 (central), as it did in other states. Here it is at full strength from the first year.
sensitivity_cases.change_as_recorded: no ramp (full rate from 2027; Madison's observed path unchanged)

sensitivity_cases.label: Rural places and small communities held at the minimum rate
sensitivity_cases.what: Rural areas and small communities, which have no measured activity, get only the minimum rate set from Madison's permits (0.2345 per 1,000 single-family homes per year) instead of their level from the statewide estimate. Shows how much of the addition comes from those places.
sensitivity_cases.change_as_recorded: rural and small-community places at the Madison floor (0.2345)

sensitivity_cases.label: Count per eligible property, not per single-family home
sensitivity_cases.what: Rates are divided by the properties each state's law makes eligible (houses plus small multifamily properties) instead of by single-family homes. A separate model with its own baseline (636 permits); it was run at Gate 3 (Milwaukee on its assumed ramp) and is not rerun here, and its 10th-percentile lower is left out because the adopted lower is defined differently.
sensitivity_cases.change_as_recorded: eligible-property basis without one-unit attached homes: permits per 1,000 properties eligible under each state's law (detached homes plus multifamily properties)

sensitivity_cases.label: The law multiplies today's rates (instead of lifting places to other states' levels)
sensitivity_cases.what: Each place's current rate is multiplied by one statewide factor, instead of rising to the level that similar places reached in the eight statewide-law states. Places that permit almost nothing today would stay near zero. Before-and-after counts in other states contradict this, but no Midwest state has data after a statewide law yet.
sensitivity_cases.change_as_recorded: multiplicative: the law only multiplies each place's current rate by the pooled statewide-law factor
sensitivity_cases.source: scripts/run_pooled_revision.py multiplicative(), refitted on the adopted current-law rates

sensitivity_cases.label: Predict Wisconsin from California's cities only
sensitivity_cases.what: Wisconsin places are predicted from a model fitted on California cities alone, where cities like Madison responded weakly. A downside case.
sensitivity_cases.change_as_recorded: California-only market regression (refitted on cap+A2 counts)
sensitivity_cases.source: scripts/run_pooled_revision.py ca_only_regression(), on the adopted current-law rates

sensitivity_cases.label: Places with uncoded rules behave like prohibited places
sensitivity_cases.what: Places whose ADU rules have not been coded (69% of single-family homes) behave like places that prohibit ADUs, instead of like places that restrict them. Changes only the current-law baseline; the law's addition moves the other way by about as much.
sensitivity_cases.change_as_recorded: Places with uncoded rules behave like prohibited places
sensitivity_cases.source: engine with only the current-law rate changed (reference/adu_model_baseline_only_effects.csv, case uncoded-prohibited)

sensitivity_cases.label: No ramp for recently liberalized places (full current-law rate at once)
sensitivity_cases.what: Places that loosened their ADU rules recently are at their new group's rate at once, instead of rising to it over a few years. Changes only the current-law baseline.
sensitivity_cases.change_as_recorded: No ramp for recently liberalized places (full current-law rate at once)
sensitivity_cases.source: engine with only the current-law rate changed (reference/adu_model_baseline_only_effects.csv, case no-baseline-ramp)

sensitivity_cases.label: Madison's current-law rate = its 2026 pace so far (provisional)
sensitivity_cases.what: Madison's current-law rate is its 2026 pace so far (42 second homes, 1 January to 23 October, provisional) instead of its 2022-2025 rate. Changes only the current-law baseline; Madison's addition falls by about as much.
sensitivity_cases.change_as_recorded: Madison's current-law rate = its 2026 pace so far (provisional)
sensitivity_cases.source: engine with only the current-law rate changed (reference/adu_model_baseline_only_effects.csv, case madison-2026)

sensitivity_cases.what: Madison's current-law rate uses 2024-2025 only. Changes only the current-law baseline.
sensitivity_cases.source: engine with only the current-law rate changed (reference/adu_model_baseline_only_effects.csv, case madison-2024-2025)

sensitivity_cases.what: Madison's 2022-2025 rate leaves out the one builder's programme of second homes. Changes only the current-law baseline.

sensitivity_cases.what: Milwaukee rises from its pre-reform rate to Madison's rate within about four years of its August 2025 ADU reform (the assumed ramp used at Gate 3), instead of staying at its measured 2022-2025 rate. Changes only the current-law baseline; Milwaukee's addition falls by about as much.

sensitivity_cases.source: engine with only the current-law rate changed (reference/adu_model_baseline_only_effects.csv, case milwaukee-ramp)

sensitivity_cases.label: Wisconsin's baseline rises like no-law places (×1.11 a year)
sensitivity_cases.what: Every Wisconsin place's current-law rate keeps rising as fast as in cities and states without a statewide ADU law: those rose about 1.5 times from their before-period to their after-period, four years later (about ×1.11 a year), almost entirely because of local reforms there. Wisconsin's main local reform (Madison 2021) is already in its measured rate, so this is a check rather than the main case. Changes only the current-law baseline; the law's addition falls by nearly as much.

local_effects.text: Each place's rate with the law comes from what similar places reached in the statewide-law states (by home values, incomes and size), not from its current local rules. So if a city's rules are coded wrong, its current-law baseline is wrong, and the law's addition there moves by about the same amount the other way; the total with the law barely moves. Coding errors change the split between baseline and addition much more than the number of permits expected with the law.
local_effects.example: Example: if every place with uncoded rules behaved like places that prohibit ADUs, the baseline would fall by 186 permits over 2027–2031, the addition would rise by 159, and the total with the law would fall by 28 (0.3% of 9,361; central scenario).
local_effects.not_computed: Re-coding individual places one at a time has not been run as separate cases.

addition.title: Cases that change what the law adds statewide
addition.intro: Each changes one part of how the law's effect is estimated from other states.

baseline.title: Cases that change only today's rates (the baseline)
baseline.intro: Each changes the current-law rate of some places. A higher baseline means a smaller addition by nearly the same amount, so the total with the law moves much less.

local.title: How individual cities' rules are coded: shifts permits between baseline and addition, not the total with the law
local.intro: Being wrong about a city's current ADU rules changes its baseline, not its rate with the law.

challenges.title: No Midwest state has data after a statewide law
challenges.text: Under current law the model expects Wisconsin to permit 0.07 per 1,000 single-family homes per year in 2027–2031 (605 permits ÷ 1,839.569 thousand homes ÷ 5 years); there is no observed statewide ADU series. States with before-and-after data (California, Rhode Island, Washington, Vermont) reached similar first-year levels however low they started, but they are coastal or New England markets. Iowa's first full year (2026) will be the first Midwest test.

challenges.title: Cities like Madison grew at a little over half the central scenario's rate in their first three years
challenges.text: Medians of 0.45, 0.54 and 0.60 permits per 1,000 single-family homes per year in 9 Washington and Oregon cities similar to Madison, against the central scenario's statewide 0.77, 0.95, 0.99. Only Madison is put on that path, so Madison's rate with the law sits below its suburbs'. If Wisconsin's other mid-size cities behave like those cities, the central is too high in its first three years; if Madison behaves like the statewide estimate, Madison is too low. This is being reviewed.

challenges.title: The hold-out test rests on 7 states
challenges.text: Keeping California in the eight states' typical level predicts the 7 other states better in 66% of resamples of those 7 states, which is within noise. The lower and strong adoption scenarios rest on how 8 states differ, one of them California.
